title: ‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
summary:
The US blockade of Iranian ports is having a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive.
Share ‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant on social mediaTehran, Iran – Iran’s economy is expected to contract further due to the ongoing blockade of its ports by the United States, inflicting pain on tens of millions of Iranians.
The US believes its naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and sanctions – part of its maximum pressure campaign on Tehran – are working.
Strikes on US interests in the region this week, including radar systems in Bahrain, have been viewed as a defiant response to the US military and economic pressure.
Tehran-based economist Peyman Molavi said if current conditions persist, Iran’s inflation could rise considerably over the coming months.

title: Ed Miliband: EU deal not dependent on tuition fees agreement
summary:
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".
He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."

title: Photos: Genocide ruling spotlights human toll of 2017 Rohingya crisis
summary:
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, finding the military acted with “genocidal intent” and killed about 10,000 people during its 2017 operations in Rakhine state.
In a landmark judgement under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar in breach of its obligations — a decision Rohingya activists hope will finally bring accountability for years of mass killings, rapes and the burning of villages.
Nearly a million Rohingya fled those attacks, crossing into Bangladesh and building one of the world’s largest refugee settlements around Cox’s Bazar.
Today, many remain confined to overcrowded, fragile camps, stateless and with little prospect of safe return, even as the ICJ ruling sharpens pressure on Myanmar’s military and raises wider questions about justice for victims of mass atrocities.
This photo story returns to the early months of the crisis in 2017, documenting Rohingya families arriving exhausted and traumatised, queuing for food and trying to rebuild a semblance of community in the makeshift camps.

title: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
summary:

And, Army delays lead azide detonation in IowaGood morning.
Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill.
The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23.

title: Trump greets 'my friend' Putin as pair share handshake
summary:
Donald Trump has called Vladimir Putin his "friend" ahead of a meeting with China's President Xi in Shenzhen.
The pair were seen sharing a friendly handshake, with the US president saying they have a "great relationship".
According to Putin's top foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, the war in Ukraine was the main topic of the meeting, which lasted 35 to 40 minutes.
The two leaders also discussed US-Russia bilateral relations.

title: Backing Trump, US Senate Republicans block Iran war resolution
summary:
The Senate voted 51 ‌to 48, largely along party lines, to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House of Representatives.
Only three Republicans - Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky - voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution.
Trump's fellow Republicans, who rarely break with the president, stood behind him in support of the US-Israeli war ⁠on Iran that started on February 28.

title: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict
summary:
By Stine Jacobsen and Tom LittleCOPENHAGEN, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Denmark's parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future ‌that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after US President ‌Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.
The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark's foreign ministry tells the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.
DIFFICULT TIME FOR GREENLANDERSNaaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, said Trump's pressure had led to distrust in Greenland towards the US administration.
Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize ‌the situation in Greenland.

title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
summary:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

title: Bernie Sanders: A Foreign Policy for the Many
summary:
Politics / Bernie Sanders: A Foreign Policy for the Many From military spending to climate change, the senator makes the case for a foreign policy rooted in democracy and our common humanity.
For too long, US foreign policy has been shaped by a narrow consensus that serves the powerful few rather than the democratic many.
Both outcomes—apathy and authoritarianism—erode the foundations of democracy and threaten the universal human rights that should anchor any just foreign policy.
A progressive foreign policy must therefore begin with moral clarity.
We must also articulate an affirmative vision: a foreign policy that confronts global oligarchy, strengthens democratic institutions, and builds genuine partnerships.

title: Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war
summary:
Share Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war on social mediaIslamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, arrived in New Delhi on Friday, becoming the first Pakistani federal minister to visit India since the neighbours fought a four-day war in May 2025.
It is the first such visit since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari travelled to Goa in May 2023.
The choice of ministerIndian media, quoting diplomatic sources, reported that India’s invitation was for Pakistan’s minister for national heritage and culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi.
Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on November 6 only that it had received an invitation and would decide after consultations.
In September this year, Alok Dimri, India’s SCO coordinator, spent three days in Islamabad and shook hands with Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar.
